extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in political economy and church–state relations
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic guidance and historical argument about how states can manage the moral, political, and temporal power of religious orders; discusses remedies, institutional arrangements, and consequences for public tranquillity and sovereign security. Draws on European historical examples (medieval–early modern church, papacy, Reformation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Small religious sects enforce moral regularity via internal sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: In little religious sects the morals of the common people have been almost always remarkably regular and orderly; expulsion or excommunication punishes scandal and enforces austere morals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that sectary discipline (excommunication/expulsion) creates social pressure that curbs profligacy and enforces regular conduct, though such morals can be 'disagreeably rigorous and unsocial.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy — universal study of science and philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: The state might render almost universal among all people of middling or more than middling rank and fortune the study of science and philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend requiring probationary examinations (even in higher sciences) before one may exercise liberal professions or hold offices, not by merely giving salaries to teachers; 'Science is the great antidote to the poison of enthusiasm and superstition.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy — encourage frequent and gay public diversions
rubrics_metrics.description: The state should give liberty to those who would amuse and divert the people by painting, poetry, music, dancing, and dramatic representations and exhibitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such diversions dissipate melancholy and gloomy humour (the nurse of superstition), inspire gaiety and good humour inconsistent with fanaticism, and dramatic performances expose artifices to ridicule, making them objects of fanatical abhorrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality of law toward religions
rubrics_metrics.description: In a country where the law favoured the teachers of no one religion more than those of another, it would not be necessary that any of them should have immediate dependency upon the sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the state is neutral, sovereign's role is limited to keeping the peace among religious teachers and preventing persecution or oppression among them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of an established/governing religion to sovereign security
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is an established or governing religion the sovereign can never be secure unless he has the means of influencing in a considerable degree the greater part of the teachers of that religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because clergy as an incorporated body can act in concert and their interests often differ from the sovereign's, they can propagate doctrines subversive of sovereign authority and threaten civil order; influence rather than impotence is necessary for security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy as a corporate interest often opposes sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: The clergy of every established church constitute a great incorporation; their interest as an incorporated body is never the same with that of the sovereign, and is sometimes directly opposite to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their authority depends on the supposed certainty of doctrine and demands implicit faith; any sovereign doubt or protection of dissenters provokes clerical sanction and popular transfer of allegiance to more orthodox rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force is a poor instrument against clergy; prefer persuasion and preferment
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear is in almost all cases a wretched instrument of government, and ought in particular never to be employed against any order of men who have the smallest pretensions to independency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violence makes clergy and doctrine more popular; management and persuasion are safer and easier; sovereigns should influence clergy through preferment and the expectations/fears that come with office rather than by force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical benefices as life-tenure require careful handling
rubrics_metrics.description: In all Christian churches, the benefices of the clergy are a sort of freeholds ... they enjoy, not during pleasure, but during life or good behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irregular or violent deprivation of benefices will render clergy and doctrine more popular and dangerous; precarious tenure could make clergy appear mercenary and undermine confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal centralization created a 'spiritual army' dangerous to sovereigns
rubrics_metrics.description: The pope gradually drew to himself the collation of almost all bishoprics and abbacies ... forming clergy into a spiritual army directed by one head and conducted upon one uniform plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This made clergy in different countries dependent on a foreign sovereign (the pope) and capable of coordinated action against temporal sovereigns; their wealth and jurisdictions made them formidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic development weakens temporal clerical power
rubrics_metrics.description: The gradual improvements of arts, manufactures, and commerce ... destroyed ... the whole temporal power of the clergy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arts and commerce enabled clergy to spend revenues on themselves (reducing charity, hospitality, and retainers), grant leases increasing tenant independence, thereby dissolving ties of interest and weakening clerical temporal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoring election rights for church offices increases state influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Sovereigns endeavoured to recover the influence ... by procuring to the deans and chapters ... the restoration of their ancient right of electing the bishop; and to the monks ... that of electing the abbot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-establishing these ancient electoral procedures, combined with sovereign consent and approval, gave states indirect means to influence clerical appointments and thereby reduce papal control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal concordats/pragmatic sanctions can restrain papal power
rubrics_metrics.description: The concordat ... gave to the kings of France the absolute right of presenting to all the great ... benefices of the Gallican church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal agreements between state and papacy (or statutes) can modify collation rights and create a clergy more independent of Rome and more disposed to support the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episcopal system (Lutheran/Anglican) favors peace and loyalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Followers of Luther ... preserved more or less of the episcopal government, established subordination among the clergy, gave the sovereign the disposal of all the bishoprics ... This system of church government was, from the beginning, favourable to peace and good order, and to submission to the civil sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the sovereign controls major ecclesiastical appointments, clergy tend to court the sovereign and higher ranks, cultivating learning and decorum rather than popular fanaticism; it has 'never been the occasion of any tumult or civil commotion' where established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular election of pastors (Calvinist practice) tends to disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: The followers of Calvin ... bestowed upon the people of each parish the right of electing their own pastor; as long as the people preserved this right, it seems to have been productive of nothing but disorder and confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular elections were often conducted under clerical influence, encouraging fanaticism; parish appointments could trigger violent contests, schisms, and factional political disturbances, especially in small republics, so magistrates often assumed presentation rights to preserve peace.
